The '''Caribbean pine''' ('''''Pinus caribaea''''') is a hard [[pine]] species native to [[Central America]], southeastern Mexico, and the northern [[West Indies]] (in [[Cuba]], [[the Bahamas]], and the [[Turks and Caicos Islands]]). It belongs to subsection ''[[Pinus subsect. Australes|Australes]]'' in subgenus ''[[Pinus subg. Pinus|Pinus]]''. It inhabits [[tropical and subtropical coniferous forests]] such as [[Bahamian pineyards]], in both lowland [[savanna]]s and montane forests.

==Taxonomy==
As of 2026, the species has three accepted [[variety (biology)|varieties]]:<ref name=powo/>
*''Pinus caribaea'' var. ''caribaea'' – '''Caribbean pine''', '''''pino macho''''', '''pitch pine''' ([[Pinar del Río Province]] and [[Isla de la Juventud]] in western Cuba)
*''Pinus caribaea'' var. ''bahamensis'' <small>(Grisebach) W.H.Barrett & Golfari</small> – '''Bahamas pine''', '''Caicos pine''' ([[The Bahamas]], Turks and Caicos Islands)
*''Pinus caribaea'' var. ''hondurensis'' <small>(Sénéclauze) W.H.Barrett & Golfari</small> – '''Honduras pine''', '''Nicaragua pine''' (states of [[Quintana Roo]] and the [[Yucatán]] in [[Mexico]], [[Belize]], [[Guatemala]], [[El Salvador]], [[Honduras]], [[Nicaragua]]). Treated a separate species, ''Pinus hondurensis'' <small>Sénéclauze</small>, by some authors.<ref name="Businský">{{cite journal |last1=Businský |first1=Roman |title=The Genus ''Pinus'' L., Pines – contribution to knowledge |journal=Acta Pruhoniciana |date=2008 |volume=88 |pages=1-126 |language=cs}}</ref> It differs markedly from vars. ''caribaea'' and ''bahamensis'' in having larger cones with a prominent transverse ridge on the apophyses and stouter spike-like umbo (rather than small prickles),<ref name="Businský"/><ref name="Loock">{{cite book |last1=Loock |first1=E. E. M. |title=The Pines of Mexico and British Honduras |date=1950 |pages=210-213|oclc=3510213|publisher=Government Printer}}</ref><ref name="Lückhoff">{{cite journal |last1=Lückhoff |first1=H. A. |title=The natural distribution, growth and botanical variation of ''Pinus caribaea'' and its cultivation in South Africa |journal=Annale Universiteit van Stellenbosch |date=1964 |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=3-108}}</ref> and in the seedlings retaining glaucous single juvenile leaves for nine months to a year or more, as opposed to three to four months in the other two varieties.<ref name="Lückhoff"/> The seedling growth rate is also significantly faster.<ref name="Lückhoff"/>

==Distribution==
It has been proposed that the pines of ''Australes'' subsection (of which Caribbean pine is part) arrived to the Caribbean basin from the [[southeastern United States]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Adams|first1=D. C.|last2=Jackson|first2=J. F.|year=1997|title=A phylogenetic analysis of the southern pines (''Pinus'' subsect. ''Australes'' Loudon): biogeographical and ecological implications|journal=Proceedings of the Biological Society of Washington|volume=110|issue=4|pages=681–692|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/part/48755|via=Biodiversity Heritage Library|access-date=7 October 2025}}</ref> Regarding the population in the Bahamas, it has been proposed that this species emigrated into the region from Florida four or five thousand years ago, long after the end of the [[Last Glacial Period|Ice Age]], as the climate became wetter. Based on fossil species assemblages it is believed that the environment on the Bahamas was much less forested and a dry savannah during the glacial maximum some 18,000 years ago when the sea level was some {{convert|120|m|abbr=off}} lower than it is today.<ref name=Olson1982>{{cite journal |last1=Olson |first1=Storrs L. |last2=Pregill |first2=Gregory K. |date=1982 |title=Fossil Vertebrates from the Bahamas — Introduction to the Paleontology of Bahaman Vertebrates |url=https://repository.si.edu/bitstream/handle/10088/15601/vz_Bahamas_fossils.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y |journal=Smithsonian Contributions to Paleobiology |volume=48 |pages=1–7 |doi=10.5479/si.00810266.48.1 |s2cid=4838349 |access-date=2 March 2020}}</ref><ref name=Pregill1982>{{cite journal |last=Pregill |first=Gregory K. |date=1982 |title=Fossil Vertebrates from the Bahamas — Fossil Amphibians and Reptiles from New Providence Island, Bahamas |url=https://repository.si.edu/bitstream/handle/10088/15601/vz_Bahamas_fossils.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y |journal=Smithsonian Contributions to Paleobiology |volume=48 |pages=19–20 |access-date=2 March 2020}}</ref>

Paleoclimatic<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Dvorak|first1=W. S.|last2=Hamrick|first2=J. L.|last3=Gutierrez|first3=E. A.|year=2005|title=The origin of Caribbean pine in the seasonal swamps of the Yucatán|journal=International Journal of Plant Sciences|volume=166|pages=985-994|issue=6|doi=10.1086/449314}}</ref> and genetic data<ref name=jardon>{{cite journal|last1=Jardón-Barbolla|first1=L.|last2=Delgado-Valerio|first2=P.|last3=Geada-López|first3=G.|last4=Vázquez-Lobo|first4=A.|last5=Pinero|first5=D.|year=2011|title=Phylogeography of ''Pinus'' subsection ''Australes'' in the Caribbean Basin|journal=Annals of Botany|volume=107|issue=2|pages=229-241|doi=10.1093/aob/mcq232}}</ref> have been used to propose that ''P. caribaea'' ultimately originated in Central America. According to chloroplast genetic data, ''P. caribaea'' lineages colonized the Caribbean islands from populations in Central America at least twice (one leading to Cuban populations and another leading to the populations on the Bahamas).<ref name=jardon/>

Fossils are known from the Pleistocene of Florida.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Berry |first=Edward W. |date=October 1917 |title=The Fossil Plants from Vero, Florida |url=https://doi.org/10.1086/622533 |journal=The Journal of Geology |volume=25 |issue=7 |pages=661–666 |doi=10.1086/622533 |issn=0022-1376|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Ecology==
Periodic [[wildfire]]s play a major role in the distribution of this species; this tree regenerates quickly and aggressively, replacing broadleaf trees after fires. In zones without fires, the [[Ecological succession|succession]] continues and the pine forest is replaced by tropical broadleaf forest. The young pines require bright sunlight to grow, and are resistant to fire once they mature.<ref name=CONABIO>{{Cite web| url=http://www.conabio.gob.mx/conocimiento/info_especies/arboles/doctos/55-pinac2m.pdf| title=Árboles y arbustos potencialmente valiosos para la restauración ecológica y la reforestación. |last1=Vázquez-Yanes|first1=C.|first2=A. I.|last2=Batis Muñoz|first3=M. I.|last3=Alcocer Silva|first4=M.|last4=Gual Díaz|first5=C.|last5=Sánchez Dirzo | name-list-style= amp| year= 1999|language=es}}</ref><ref name="commonwealth">{{cite web |url=http://www.bahamas.gov.bs/BahamasWeb/VisitingTheBahamas.nsf/Subjects/Ecosystems+Of+The+Bahamas |title=Ecosystems Of The Bahamas |publisher=The Commonwealth of The Bahamas |access-date=2009-01-15}}</ref>

==Conservation==
According to the [[International Union for Conservation of Nature]], this species as a whole is considered of [[least concern]],<ref name="iucn status 12 November 2021" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.conifers.org/pi/Pinus_caribaea.php|title=Pinus caribaea (pino macho) description - The Gymnosperm Database|website=www.conifers.org|access-date=2018-08-23}}</ref> but two of the three varieties are considered [[Endangered species|endangered]] (var. ''caribaea'')<ref>{{cite iucn |author=Farjon, A. |date=2013 |title=''Pinus caribaea'' var. ''caribaea'' |volume=2013 |article-number=e.T34184A2849737 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2013-1.RLTS.T34184A2849737.en |access-date=12 November 2021}}</ref> or [[Vulnerable species|vulnerable]] (var. ''bahamensis'').<ref>{{cite iucn |author=Sanchez, M. |author2=Hamilton, M.A. |author3=Farjon, A. |date=2013 |title=''Pinus caribaea'' var. ''bahamensis'' |volume=2013 |article-number=e.T20364362A20402659 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2013-1.RLTS.T20364362A20402659.en |access-date=12 November 2021}}</ref>

==Uses==
Lumber and pulpwood from this tree shipped to Florida is the main export of the [[Abaco Islands]].<ref name=Colliers>{{cite encyclopedia|last1=Bower|first1=Paul|editor-first=Bernard|editor-last=Johnston|encyclopedia=Collier's Encyclopedia |title=Abaco Islands|edition= First |year=1997|publisher=P.F. Collier|volume=I A to Ameland|location=New York, NY|page=4}}</ref>

The Uverito forest in [[Venezuela]], located between the states of [[Anzoátegui]] and [[Monagas]], is the largest artificial forest in the world planted by man, with around {{convert|600000|ha|acre}} of Caribbean pine forest plantations.
